findings: The frozen repository context contains three equivalent IPC-list source questions. The answer directly addresses common IPC mechanisms while explicitly binding detailed semantics to Unix/Linux rather than pretending to enumerate every operating-system facility.

The Linux man-pages source packet supports the answer's model distinctions: pipes/FIFOs as bounded unidirectional channels, POSIX/System V message queues as message-oriented exchange, shared memory as a shared mapped region, semaphores as synchronization, AF_UNIX sockets as local process communication, and signals as asynchronous notifications/control.

The answer is stronger than a name list because it organizes IPC into data-channel, shared-state and control/synchronization models, then explains the mechanism that creates each tradeoff. This satisfies the concept requirement to explain not only definitions but why the choices differ.

Important boundaries are correctly preserved: FIFO pathnames are rendezvous names rather than ordinary payload files; portable pipe semantics are treated as unidirectional; shared memory is not claimed universally fastest; shared memory needs explicit synchronization; semaphores are not bulk-data channels; local message queues are not conflated with distributed brokers; AF_UNIX proves that sockets are also local IPC.

The selection guidance is workload-dependent and covers payload shape, message boundaries, related versus unrelated processes, local client/server topology, synchronization complexity, backpressure, lifecycle and portability without inventing benchmark numbers or personal production claims.

The followups are source-specific and test common misconceptions about shared-memory synchronization, pipe versus FIFO discovery, queue versus stream semantics, Unix sockets, signals and semaphores. The three-minute section is significantly longer than literal oral timing, so oral quality is scored 4/5 despite strong modular structure.
